transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, I just... I don't know. I guess I'm here because I just can't keep going on like this, especially at work. I do installation and maintenance, mostly commercial repair stuff, you know, heavy equipment, electrical panels, that sort of thing. Been doing it for years, ever since I left high school. You get used to the noise on a job site, or at least you're supposed to. But lately, what really brought me in is... I just can't stop jumping out of my skin. 

I mean, literally jumping. If I'm working on a panel and a breaker snaps, or if one of the other guys drops a tool on the concrete—which happens all the time because these new guys just don't hold onto their gear—I just about hit the ceiling. It's like a live wire goes right through my spine. And it's not even just the loud noises, either. If I'm bent over fixing a unit and somebody just comes up behind me to ask a question or hand me something, I practically jump out of my work boots. 

And the thing is, the absolute worst part of it, is that my heart just keeps hammering and hammering afterward. Like, pounding so hard I can feel it in my throat and hear it in my ears, and it stays like that for a long, long time. Long after everyone else has just moved on and gone back to what they were doing, I'm still standing there trying to get my chest to stop thumping over a dropped wrench. They're all just looking at me, and I'm just trying to catch my breath. It's embarrassing, honestly, and it's just... it's exhausting living like this every single shift.
Are there any specific situations or places where you feel like you're more likely to have these jumping and heart pounding episodes?

Well, yeah, absolutely. I mean, it's gotten to the point where... I just can't go near certain things anymore. Like, if the dispatcher sends me a ticket for a specific type of industrial breaker—the big ones, you know, the heavy 480-volt panels—I'll just... I'll make up an excuse. I'll tell the foreman my work truck is acting up, or I left my insulated tools back at the shop, or I'll just straight up say I'm backed up on another job and try to trade tickets with one of the other guys. I've been doing that a lot lately, just making up whatever I can think of. 

And there are certain job sites, too, especially the older commercial basements or the cramped mechanical rooms. I'll pull up to the address, see the building, and I just won't go in. I'll literally sit in my truck, gripping the steering wheel, trying to talk myself into it, and then I just end up calling in sick or saying I had a family emergency. 

I just make excuses not to go near those certain panels, the big breakers, those specific job sites... or even to let anybody talk about that day. If one of the guys brings it up, or asks what happened, I just walk away. I have to. Because if I go near that stuff, or if I let myself even start talking about it, the memories just start up in my head. It's like a movie starts playing, and once it starts, I can’t shut it off. It just loops and loops, and that's when the jumping and the heart pounding gets completely out of control. So I just spend half my shift figuring out how to dodge all those things, because if I don't, my brain just gets stuck on it for the rest of the day and I'm completely useless.
Is there something specific that happened to you on one of these job sites that you think might be connected to when these symptoms started?

Well, yeah... yeah, there was. It's... it's been going on for a while now. About a year and a month, actually. It was on this retrofit job, an older commercial building downtown. We were supposed to be swapping out some old gear, upgrading the main distribution panel, you know? And... well, there was an arc-flash accident. 

I don't know if you know much about electrical work, doc, but an arc-flash isn't just a spark. It's an explosion. It's literally a bomb going off in your face. The temperature can get up to like, 35,000 degrees in a fraction of a second, hotter than the surface of the sun, and the sound... the sound is like a shotgun going off right next to your ear. We had the power supposedly locked out, tagged out, the whole nine yards, standard procedure. I was in there, working on the busbars, and my buddy, Dave... he was right next to me. 

And then, just... boom. A blinding flash of light, white and blue, and this shockwave that just picked me up and threw me backward into the concrete wall. I remember the smell of burning ozone and... and burning hair. And the noise, my ears were just ringing so loud I couldn't hear myself screaming. Dave took the brunt of it. He... he was in the hospital for months, skin grafts, the whole thing. I got lucky, physically, anyway. Just some minor burns on my arms and a concussion from hitting the wall. 

But since that day, a year and a month ago... that's when it all started. The jumping, the heart pounding, the... the movies playing in my head. Every time I see a panel like that one, or smell something metallic, or hear a loud crack, I'm right back in that basement. I can see the flash, I can smell the smoke, I can hear Dave... I just... I can't shake it. It's been over a year, and it feels like it happened yesterday. I just can't get that day out of my head, doc. It's ruined everything.
Do you find yourself avoiding people, places, or activities that remind you of the arc-flash accident?

Yeah, I mean, like I was saying before... I just... I do everything I can to stay away from it all. It's not just a passing thought, doc, it's like a full-time job just trying to figure out how to not be anywhere near those things. 

Like, if I see a 480-volt panel, or even if I just hear that we're bidding on a job that involves those big industrial breakers, my stomach just completely drops out. I'll make up any excuse in the book. I'll say I'm sick, I'll say my truck is broken down, I'll say I lost my specialized tools, whatever it takes to not have to go near them. And it's the same with the job sites themselves. Those cramped mechanical rooms, the older basements with the concrete walls... I'll pull up, look at the building, and I just can't make my legs work to go inside. I'll sit in the truck for twenty minutes, sweating, gripping the wheel, and then I'll just call the dispatcher and say I've got a family emergency and I have to go home.

And it's not just the places or the equipment, either. It's the guys, too. If anyone even brings up that day, or asks how Dave is doing, or tries to talk about arc-flash safety protocols... I just have to walk away. I can't even stand to hear the words. Because the second I let myself get near those panels, or those basements, or even just let someone talk about it... it's like a switch flips in my brain. The movie starts playing, the flash, the noise, the smell... and once it starts in my head, I just can't shut it off. It just keeps looping and looping, and my heart starts hammering, and I'm just completely done for the rest of the day. So yeah, I avoid all of it. I have to, or I wouldn't survive a single shift.
Do you ever experience flashbacks to the arc-flash accident when you're not trying to think about it?

Oh, man... yeah. Yeah, absolutely. That’s... honestly, that’s the worst part of this whole thing, because you’d think if I just avoid the heavy gear, if I just stay away from the basements and keep my head down, I’d be safe, right? But it doesn't work like that. It doesn't matter how hard I try to keep my mind on something else, or how normal the day is going. It just comes out of absolutely nowhere. 

I could be doing the most basic, mindless stuff. Like, I could just be standing out in the parking lot at the shop, completely away from any live power, just... just loading tools in the truck. Minding my own business, maybe thinking about what I'm going to grab for lunch or what traffic is going to be like on the way home. And then, bam. Without any warning at all, I’ll just see that flash right in my head. That blinding white and blue light, it just takes over my vision. And I'll hear the trainee yelling—that awful, awful screaming—and it just... it knocks me completely sideways. 

I literally have to grab onto the side of the truck bed to keep my balance, because my brain is telling me the explosion just happened. It feels exactly like it’s happening again, right in that very second. It's not like a normal memory where you know it's in the past. I'm right back in that cramped room, bracing for the shockwave to throw me into the concrete wall. I'll just be standing there in the sunshine, gripping the side of my truck, completely losing my mind over something that isn't even there. It just ambushes me, doc. I never know when it's going to hit, and it's exhausting just waiting for it to happen.
Do you have nightmares about the arc-flash accident?

Nightmares... yeah. Sleep is... honestly, sleep is just a joke these days, doc. It's a whole ordeal. Most nights, I don't even get to the nightmare part right away because I can't even get my eyes to stay shut. I'll just be lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and the house gets so quiet, you know? But then my brain starts playing tricks on me. I’m up half the night just... listening. I'll be straining my ears because I keep thinking I hear these little pops, or this faint buzzing sound coming from inside the bedroom walls. 

Like, I know the wiring in my house is fine, I know what good wiring sounds like, and I've checked my own panel a hundred times just to be sure, but my brain just won't let it go. I just lay there, tense as a board, waiting for the walls to blow out. 

And then... when my body finally just gives out from sheer exhaustion and I do manage to drift off... that's when it gets me. I don't even know if you can call them regular nightmares, it's more like a time machine. I'll shoot straight up in bed, and I'm just completely drenched. I wake up sweating so bad my shirt is glued to my chest and the sheets are soaked, and I'm just gasping for air. For a good five, ten minutes, I don't even know I'm in my own bed. I'm sweating like I’m right back on that job, right back in that cramped concrete basement, smelling the ozone and waiting for the blast to hit me. It takes me forever to realize I'm actually safe at home, and by then, my heart is going a million miles an hour and there's no way I'm falling back asleep. So I just sit up in the living room until the sun comes up. It's just... it's exhausting, doc. Every single night is like going to war.
Do you try to push away or avoid thoughts about the arc-flash accident when they come into your mind?

Yeah, I try... I try so hard, doc. I mean, like I was telling you before about making up those excuses, right? Saying my truck is busted or I lost my tools or whatever... it's all because I'm trying to push the thoughts away. I'm trying to build this... this wall in my head, you know? 

If I can just avoid those 480-volt panels, if I can just stay away from those big industrial breakers and those cramped concrete basements, then maybe I won't have to think about it. Because if I don't see it, maybe I won't think about it. And it's not just the gear or the locations. It's the talking, too. Like I said, if any of the guys even try to bring up that day, or ask about Dave, or even just start talking about safety protocols for arc-flashes... I have to shut it down immediately. I'll walk away, I'll change the subject, I'll literally put my hands over my ears if I have to. 

Because I know what happens if I let even one tiny thought about it slip through. If I let myself think about it for even a second, it's like... it's like a dam breaking. Once it starts in my head, I absolutely cannot shut it off. The whole thing just floods in—the noise, the smell of the ozone, the screaming—and I'm just drowning in it. So I spend my whole day just trying to block it out, trying to push it down, trying to think about literally anything else. I'll count the bolts on a flange, I'll recite the alphabet backwards in my head, I'll sing songs... anything to just keep my brain occupied so the thoughts don't creep in. But it's exhausting, doc. It's like trying to hold a door shut while someone is pounding on the other side, all day, every day.
Have you noticed any problems in your relationships with family or friends since the arc-flash accident?

Yeah... yeah, it’s... it's really bad, doc. I mean, my whole life has just completely derailed, and it's affecting absolutely everyone around me. My wife, Sarah, she... she tells me I’m just a ghost now. She says I'm physically sitting on the couch next to her, but I'm just a million miles away, staring at the wall, completely checked out. And she's not wrong. I can't even focus on what she's saying about her day, or the kids, or whatever, because my brain is just constantly scanning, constantly trying to make sure I don't get put in a situation that reminds me of that day. Everything in my life—every single decision I make from the minute I wake up—revolves around making sure I never have to face another blowup like that. 

And she gets frustrated, you know? Because I used to be the guy who fixed everything around the house, and now I won't even go near the breaker box if a fuse blows. I make her call an electrician for our own house. It's pathetic. 

And work... man, work is a disaster. I’ve been written up twice in the last month. Me. Written up. I’ve been with the company for fifteen years and I’ve never even had a verbal warning before this. But my boss says I'm unreliable now, because I keep making up those excuses to get out of jobs, like I told you. And the worst part is, they were grooming me for a supervisor spot. We'd been talking about it for six months. It meant a pay bump, better hours, getting off the tools a bit as I get older. But they pulled me completely out of the running last week. My manager pulled me into the office and said he needs someone who can actually show up and lead the crew, not someone who disappears or refuses to go down into the mechanical rooms. 

So yeah, my marriage is hanging by a thread because I'm barely a person anymore, my career is tanking... and I can't even blame them, doc. How can I? I wouldn't want to be around me either. I'm just so consumed by trying to avoid that... that feeling, that I'm ruining everything else I actually care about.

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been written up at work, pulled out of the running for supervisor, and my wife says I’m barely present at home because everything in my life has started revolving around avoiding another blowup like that day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the accident on my relationships with family and friends, which corresponds to the functional impairment I am experiencing, such as my wife saying I'm barely present at home.

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, it’s... it's really bad, doc. I mean, my whole life has just completely derailed, and it's affecting absolutely everyone around me. My wife, Sarah, she... she tells me I’m just a ghost now. She says I'm physically sitting on the couch next to her, but I'm just a million miles away, staring at the wall, completely checked out. And she's not wrong. I can't even focus on what she's saying about her day, or the kids, or whatever, because my brain is just constantly scanning, constantly trying to make sure I don't get put in a situation that reminds me of that day. Everything in my life—every single decision I make from the minute I wake up—revolves around making sure I never have to face another blowup like that. 

And she gets frustrated, you know? Because I used to be the guy who fixed everything around the house, and now I won't even go near the breaker box if a fuse blows. I make her call an electrician for our own house. It's pathetic. 

And work... man, work is a disaster. I’ve been written up twice in the last month. Me. Written up. I’ve been with the company for fifteen years and I’ve never even had a verbal warning before this. But my boss says I'm unreliable now, because I keep making up those excuses to get out of jobs, like I told you. And the worst part is, they were grooming me for a supervisor spot. We'd been talking about it for six months. It meant a pay bump, better hours, getting off the tools a bit as I get older. But they pulled me completely out of the running last week. My manager pulled me into the office and said he needs someone who can actually show up and lead the crew, not someone who disappears or refuses to go down into the mechanical rooms. 

So yeah, my marriage is hanging by a thread because I'm barely a person anymore, my career is tanking... and I can't even blame them, doc. How can I? I wouldn't want to be around me either. I'm just so consumed by trying to avoid that... that feeling, that I'm ruining everything else I actually care about.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of reminders, and hyperarousal, are consistent with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) following a traumatic event, specifically the arc-flash accident.
